30:
- The compiler graph shows calculations and which values they depend on. The compiler can turn one graph into several kernels.
- A CUDA Graph records GPU work so it can be submitted again with less setup. It can include several kernels and other GPU operations.
- They describe different parts of execution. Fusion combines calculations inside kernels; replay helps submit a sequence of work.
31:
- A tensor is an array of numbers. In these examples it’s on a GPU, but tensors can also live in CPU memory.
- A kernel is a program launched on the GPU. Running a model layer can involve several kernels.
- IR stands for intermediate representation. It describes a program’s operations in a form the compiler can work with.
- Lowering turns that description into forms closer to the target machine’s instructions.
- A guard checks whether a saved plan still applies to the current call.
- A graph break happens when some behavior can’t be included in the captured graph. Compilation can continue in another region afterward.
11:
- The fused kernel splits the tensor into blocks and works out where each block’s values are stored.
- It loads those values, adds the bias, applies ReLU and stores the final answers. The intermediate values stay local during that work.
- At the end of the tensor, some positions in a block may fall outside the array. A mask prevents accesses to those positions.
- This uses registers and other limited resources. If combining more work uses too much space, the kernel can slow down. That limits which combinations are useful.
15:
- Each program works on an output tile. The tile’s dimensions determine how many results that program calculates.
- To find its inputs, the program uses strides. A stride tells it how far to move through memory between neighboring entries.
- It loads input blocks, calculates their contribution and adds it to the partial sums. It keeps doing that until it has all the contributions needed for the output tile.
- Masks protect accesses near the matrix boundaries. The program stores the output once the sums are complete.
- Larger tiles can reuse more data, but they need more registers or shared memory. That can reduce how many programs run at once.
- The implementation may use a chosen schedule from a library, a compiler heuristic or autotuning. Autotuning tries candidate schedules and measures which works better.
22:
- A compiler needs to know that a change is valid for the inputs it supports.
- You may know something extra about your workload. For example, a sparsity pattern might always stay the same, or a graph might always have the same connections.
- A specialized implementation can use that information to skip work. Its correctness then depends on that information remaining true.
- The practical approach is to express the assumption through a supported interface or choose an operator that uses it. Then measure whether it helps. Removing a guard without preserving its assumptions can give incorrect results.
25:
- These logs help explain two common problems. A graph break means some behavior wasn’t captured, which can limit what the compiler optimizes together.
- A recompile means the runtime built another compiled variant. The logs can help you find which assumption changed.
- Set the logging variable shown here before starting Python, then run the workload that causes the problem.
- The fullgraph option asks for one captured graph and raises an error if a graph break prevents that. The resulting graph can still run as several kernels.
- The dynamic option tries to support more shape variation within a program. It still has constraints and guards.
- For eligible workloads, reduce-overhead can use CUDA Graphs. Max-autotune spends more preparation time choosing implementations. Which options work depends on the platform and backend.
24:
- This prompt gives the agent a clear experiment to run. It starts with profiling so the agent can find the repeated computation taking time.
- It keeps the original execution path for comparison and asks the agent to preserve weights and precision.
- The report should compare outputs, startup cost, warmed execution and memory across representative inputs.
- If the result is disappointing, the agent can inspect graph-break and recompile logs. It should also report the environment and how timing was measured.
- Changes to precision, quantization or the model itself need a separate comparison, because they can affect behavior as well as speed.
27:
- Start with the torch.compile tutorial and try it on a model you already have. Compare the original and compiled versions.
- Once that works, inspect a graph break or a recompilation. It helps connect the runtime behavior to the assumptions we discussed.
- For kernel details, start with Triton vector addition and then work through matrix multiplication.
- The PyTorch compiler paper goes further into capture and lowering. The CUDA guides explain hardware limits, and CUDA Graph Trees covers replay and memory management.
- The final slide also links to the OpenAI sources and model examples.
